author: Augustinus (pseudo)

passages.original: 5. Pnlientia, Dei res est. Cum patientia curramus,: non stemus, sed nec perturbemur : sed cum patientia, Quid ergo? tua est patientia? Absit. Andi beatum martyrem Cyprianum : in quodam apitulo suo sic ait, « Patientia, Dei res est » (Serm.de Bono patien- tiæ). Unde hoc ipse de Spiritu sancto per David,Tu es patientia mea. Et ut ostenderet qua curreret, et quo pervenit : Domine, inquit, spes mea a juventute mea (Psal. LXX, 5). Dicens autem multiplicem nubem testium Paulus, obtulit solem, per quem lumen videre debramus. Ait enim tanquam in tenebris constitutis : Respicientibus ad principem fidei, et perfecto- rem Jesum. Si ipse princeps, ipse perfectio; verum est quia sine nihil possumus facere.
passages.english: 5. Patience is a thing of God. Let us run with patience; let us not stand still, but neither let us be thrown into confusion, but [let us run] with patience. What then? Is the patience yours? Far from it. Hear the blessed martyr Cyprian: in a certain chapter of his he speaks thus: "Patience is a thing of God" (Sermon on the Good of Patience). Hence he himself [speaks] of this through the Holy Spirit, through David: "You are my patience." And to show by what way he was running, and where he arrived, he says: "Lord, my hope from my youth" (Psalm 70:5). And Paul, in speaking of the manifold cloud of witnesses, set before [us] the sun, through which we ought to see the light. For he says, as to those placed in darkness: "Looking to the author of faith and its perfecter, Jesus." If he himself is the author, he himself is the perfection; it is true that without [him] we can do nothing.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected: "Pnlientia" for "Patientia", "Andi" for "Audi", "apitulo" for "capitulo", "debramus" for "debeamus". "Unde hoc ipse de Spiritu sancto per David" is awkward and may be corrupt; the sense seems to be that David, speaking by the Holy Spirit, says the same thing. "Princeps fidei" (Heb. 12:2) is rendered "author of faith"; it could also be rendered "leader". "Sine nihil" lacks an object; "[him]" is supplied, after John 15:5 ("sine me"). "Dicens" is taken in the sense of "speaking of".
